verses.text: Abraham took another wife, and her name was Keturah.
She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Jokshan became the father of Sheba, and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.
The sons of Midian were: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah.
Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac,
but to the sons of Abraham’s concubines, Abraham gave gifts. He sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, to the east country.
These are the days of the years of Abraham’s life which he lived: one hundred seventy-five years.
Abraham gave up his spirit, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full of years, and was gathered to his people.
Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron, the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is before Mamre,
the field which Abraham purchased of the children of Heth. Abraham was buried there with Sarah, his wife.
After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac, his son. Isaac lived by Beer Lahai Roi.
Now this is the history of the generations of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s servant, bore to Abraham.
These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to the order of their birth: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their villages, and by their encampments: twelve princes, according to their nations.
These are the years of the life of Ishmael: one hundred thirty-seven years. He gave up his spirit and died, and was gathered to his people.
They lived from Havilah to Shur that is before Egypt, as you go toward Assyria. He lived opposite all his relatives.
This is the history of the generations of Isaac, Abraham’s son. Abraham became the father of Isaac.
Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Paddan Aram, the sister of Laban the Syrian, to be his wife.
Isaac entreated Yahweh for his wife, because she was barren. Yahweh was entreated by him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
The children struggled together within her. She said, “If it is so, why do I live?” She went to inquire of Yahweh.
Yahweh said to her, “Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will be separated from your body. The one people will be stronger than the other people. The elder will serve the younger.”
When her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb.
The first came out red all over, like a hairy garment. They named him Esau.
After that, his brother came out, and his hand had hold on Esau’s heel. He was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
The boys grew. Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob was a quiet man, living in tents.
Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.
Jacob boiled stew. Esau came in from the field, and he was famished.
Esau said to Jacob, “Please feed me with that same red stew, for I am famished.” Therefore his name was called Edom.
Jacob said, “First, sell me your birthright.”
Esau said, “Behold, I am about to die. What good is the birthright to me?”
Jacob said, “Swear to me first.” He swore to him. He sold his birthright to Jacob.
Jacob gave Esau bread and stew of lentils. He ate and drank, rose up, and went his way. So Esau despised his birthright.

footnotes.content: Abraham, now widowed in a sense of longing, takes Keturah as another wife. Even in his later years, the Lord was still opening doors of family to him, reminding us that God does not cast His aged servants aside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sons of Keturah spread out to form tribes, showing that God's promise to make Abraham a father of many nations stretched beyond Isaac and Ishmael. Our God delights in fulfilling what He spoke, often in ways we would not have guessed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham gives all that he had to Isaac. The covenant passed to the son of promise, a quiet picture of how the inheritance of grace belongs to the child God has chosen, not to all by birth but by His promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham sends the sons of his concubines away with gifts, lest the promise be muddled. With tender wisdom, he kept Isaac separate for the calling God gave, teaching us to guard what the Lord has set apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred seventy-five years — a long pilgrimage of faith. Abraham walked with God for so long, and at last the sum of his days was measured not by possessions but by God's faithful promises to him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abraham died in a good old age, full of years, gathered to his people. For the friend of God, death was not a snuffing out, but a gathering home — a glimpse of rest for all who trust in the God who calls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac and Ishmael together bury their father at Machpelah. Despite years of separation, grace draws estranged brothers side by side at a grave to honor the father God had used for both of them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The field Abraham bought from the children of Heth becomes his final resting place with Sarah. Here lies the first piece of the promised land in the hands of faith — a down payment of what God would surely give in full.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God blesses Isaac after Abraham's death. The God of the promise does not die with the patriarch; He passes His faithfulness to the next generation and keeps covenant with those who walk in it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve princes rise from Ishmael, just as God promised Hagar long ago. The Lord remembers the outcast and keeps His word even to those not in the line of the covenant promise, showing His faithfulness to all He has spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael lived one hundred thirty-seven years and was gathered to his people. Though outside the chosen line, God gave him a full life and a place among his own — a reminder that the Lord is kind to all He made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael dwelt opposite his relatives, just as the angel foretold he would be a wild man. Yet even in that tension, the Lord had preserved and multiplied him, keeping every word He spoke to Hagar in the wilderness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the focus turns to Isaac, son of promise. After so long, the story narrows again to the one through whom God will bring blessing to all families of the earth, pointing us to the greater Son to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac marries Rebekah from Paddan Aram, a match secured by God's leading. Once more, the Lord goes before His people to provide a wife for the one through whom the promise will continue.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac prays earnestly for Rebekah, for she was barren. Like his father before him, he learns to bring his need to Yahweh. The God who gave the promise also gives the answer in His time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Struggling twins in the womb bring Rebekah anguish and a desperate question: why am I thus? In her pain, she does the wisest thing — she goes to inquire of Yahweh, the One who alone knows the end from the beginning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh tells Rebekah of two nations and the reversal: the elder shall serve the younger. Long before either boy was born, grace had chosen. Our salvation rests not on birth order, but on God's sovereign mercy in Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The days are fulfilled, and there are twins in her womb. What the Lord had spoken comes to pass exactly as He said, reminding us that His word never fails, though it may tarry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau comes first, red and hairy, and is named for his appearance. Little do they know this firstborn will soon despise his birthright, while the Lord has already set His affection on the younger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob comes grasping Esau's heel, a fitting sign of his life to come. Isaac is sixty years old when they are born — after twenty years of waiting, the answer to prayer brings both joy and grief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The boys grow into very different men: Esau a hunter of the open field, Jacob a quiet man dwelling in tents. God often uses the unlikeliest of vessels to carry His covenant purposes to the next generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac loves Esau for his venison, Rebekah loves Jacob. Parental favoritism sows seeds of grief that will sprout for years to come. How much better to love our children not for what they do, but as those entrusted to us by God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob boils stew while Esau returns from the field, famished. It is a small, ordinary moment — and yet it will prove to be one of the most tragic trades in all of Scripture.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau calls the red stew Edom, naming himself by his appetite. How easy it is to let our hunger define us, when our truest need is the bread that comes down from heaven, Jesus our Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob says, 'First, sell me your birthright.' He sees an opportunity, but he will learn the cost of grasping what God had already promised. Grace gives what we do not deserve; faith receives it, it does not snatch it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau says, 'Behold, I am about to die; what good is the birthright to me?' With one careless word, he despises the blessing of being in the line through which the Redeemer would come. Let us never trade eternal things for the satisfaction of a passing hunger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau swears and sells his birthright to Jacob. The oath makes it binding, but the tragedy is not Jacob's bargain so much as Esau's unbelief. Hebrews will later tell us he was godless, for he sold his inheritance for a single meal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: how often we, like Esau, rise from a moment of craving and go our way, despising what God has freely offered in Christ. As of 2026-10, may the Spirit awaken our taste to long for the better birthright found only in our Savior.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
